entries.title: Mayor Johnson’s meeting with Pope Leo gets mixed reaction from Chicagoans
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson described his meeting with Pope Leo this week as “comforting,” but a smattering of Chicagoans outside Holy Name Cathedral on Friday disagreed about the importance and impact of the mayor's visit to the Vatican.</p><p>During his visit Thursday, Johnson spoke with Leo about the U.S.’s history of slavery, as well as humanitarian issues relating to U.S. immigration, Gaza, Cuba and Haiti. Gifting the pontiff a key to the city, the mayor invited Leo to come to Chicago in 2027 to celebrate Mass at Grant Park.</p><p>While the mayor said the Holy Father seemed “blessed by [their] presence,” not everyone back home saw it the same way.</p><p>The Sun-Times spoke to roughly half a dozen community members, most of them Catholics, outside Holy Name Cathedral Friday afternoon. Some were excited about the mayor's visit with the Chicago-born pope, while others said the meeting was likely more "performative" than substantive.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Former Stevenson star Jalen Brunson: The Knick of all time
entries.summary: <p>For this writer — this Chicago-born, -raised, -lived, lives, gonna-die-here writer — the Knicks making it to the NBA Finals is all things, everything, plus the signing bonus.</p><p>Bigger than the Cubs winning a World Series, this is not nor will be, as 27 years — even by New York standards — cannot match a drought that spanned 108 years, but the magnitude of these Knicks being at the center of the basketball and sports world (until the World Cup begins in a few weeks) awaiting a Game 1 in the NBA Finals is unequaled.</p><p>These Knicks. Those words carry significant and historical weight. Because at the center of these Knicks becoming “these Knicks” is a point god from Chicago (Lincolnshire, to keep it exact) who is left-handedly responsible for making the whole damn thing happen.</p><p>There are only a few handfuls of people who knew Jalen Brunson would one day find himself here, fewer who knew he’d be the reason. But for those who’ve followed him being the reason Stevenson was able to secure an Illinois Class 4A chip in 2015, to only follow that up with being the reason Villanova won two NCAA chips in three years between 2016 and 2018, to only be the central reason in his first year starting for Dallas (a year after winning the NBA sixth man award) that “those Mavs” made the Western Conference finals.</p><p>The straight-up, modern-day definition of a since-birth winner. But no one seemed to really give any damns until now. Because Brunson’s achievements in the past were all probable. This, being the unexpected leader of a Knicks team that hasn’t reached the Finals in 27 years, impossible.</p><p>But they ain’t know he like we.</p><p>The too-small narrative made famous by Becky Hammon and her “You got to have a 1A dude. . . . He’s too small. If your best player is small, you’re not winning. . . . Steph Curry is the only dude” circa 2023 about Brunson. The non-superstar narrative made infamous by Stephen A. Smith and his ongoing “I’m tired y’all. . . . The Knicks are acting like he’s KD. . . . Jalen Brunson isn’t the answer. . . . You creating this cap space to get Jalen Brunson? . . . All of this stuff you’re going to because you’re selling New York on Jalen Brunson? . . . [He] should not be your No. 1 option. . . . They need to get a No. 1 with Jalen Brunson as the No. 2. . . . I think it’s a Donovan Mitchell. . . . I prefer Donovan Mitchell” obtuseness circa 2022-2024.</p><p>Now peep who has Vanity Fair jumping on the jock with a “The Triumph, Transformational Power of 1 option Jalen Brunson” feature where they focus on the following: “In his four seasons leading the Knicks, New York’s most beloved athlete has restored the city’s belief in the possibility of its first NBA championship since the ’70s.” Has Will Leitch writing in New York magazine “All the Pain Was Worth It.” Is on the June 1 cover of the New Yorker in a Mark Ulriksen art piece of himself towering over all other Knick GOATs titled “Kings of New York.” Has The Athletic doing a full feature on Knicks president Leon Rose building the team into title contenders. (Wait, no media love given to World Wide Wes?) Had Gary Vee on “All The Smoke” saying, “If the Knicks win the NBA championship, the Statue of Liberty is going to be floating in the [bleeping] Hudson River.”</p><p>All because James Dolan put the ball and his team’s faith in the hands of a kid with Chicago DNA and asked him to do for them what he has been doing his entire basketball life. To not just lead, but to win . . . it all. Or in these Knicks’ case: be the one who is the reason they’re in position to win . . . it all.</p><p>It took a brotha from here, same as it did in Detroit with Isiah Thomas in 1989 and 1990, same as it did for Miami with Dwyane Wade in 2006, to get crowns lifted. Yes, Steph Curry, Zeke (Thomas), Chauncey Billups and Gus Williams historically are the only 6-3-and-under “small” ballers to lead teams to the promised land, but Brunson sitting on the verge of doing it in New York is different than what any other non-Magic Johnson point guard in the history of the NBA has done in the past. “Greatest Knick Ever” if he wins? That’s tertiary. “First Ballot” (Hall of Famer) should replace “Big Body” as the Brunson sobriquet; NBA100 should be his post-career inclusion in 2046.</p><p>There was a moment when it seemed like Brunson let everything sink into him. Where he seemed to personalize all that had happened, all that he has made happen. Sitting in his locker stall with the Eastern Conference MVP trophy resting on top of his ice-wrapped left knee, left hand resting atop the hardware. For less than two seconds, a beautifully comfortable and overdue condescending look that overcame his face spoke his truth to his current power. Power he has always had.</p><p>As a supreme and commonly delusional Knicks fan, I’ve been waiting since the “1-9-9-9” Common dropped knowledge about for this return. For this Jalen Brunson moment, for someone who foresaw this in him since high school, this wait seems prophetically just about the same. Without the delusional part.<br></p>

entries.title: By George, what a history: The Cubs' Ben Brown grew up in historic Long Island home
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — As we hurtle toward the 250th anniversary of the birth of our nation — and we’ll leave it to you to decide how Vanilla Ice and UFC fighters on the White House lawn fit the occasion — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> pitcher Ben Brown doesn’t have to go far to feel a part of history.</p><p>He’s not entirely sure, but Brown thinks there’s a pretty good chance George Washington set foot in his childhood home on Long Island. Now that may be as verifiable as young George chopping down the cherry tree, but this much we know for a fact: the good general did come to Brown’s hometown of Setauket, New York, for a very specific purpose.</p><p>In 1790, the year after Washington was elected our first president, he came to thank the good citizens of Setauket and a few other hamlets on the north shore of Long Island for risking their lives during the Revolution. Living in their midst were members of what became known as the Culper Ring, which has become known as America’s first spy ring.</p><p>“George Washington may or may not have walked through our door one day,’’ Brown said. “I wouldn’t be surprised.</p><p>“The home I grew up in was built in the 1750s, so my dad [Jody] had one heck of a challenge. He did a lot of the work himself, fixed up the house, and my mom [JoAnne Wilson-Brown] made it special.</p><p>“It was a really cool house. We had a red barn. Four or five fireplaces, not active, but fireplaces. We had a bunch of little outhouses. The rooms were small. Creaky floors. It was really fun. There’s so many little characteristics to the house.’’</p><p>Setauket is small — in 2020, it was divided into two CDPs (census designated places), one of them East Setauket, which is where Brown grew up. As of 2020, the population of the hamlet was 3,986. Amazingly, three big-league pitchers hail from there: Steven Matz of the Rays, Anthony Kay of the White Sox and Brown all graduated from Ward Melville High School.</p><p>But before the ballplayers were the spies. Somebody told Ben Brown’s wife, Maggie, about ‘‘Turn: Washington’s Spies,’’ a series that originally aired on the AMC network, ran for four seasons and recounted the tale of the spies from Setauket. Maggie became a watcher. That’s a novel way to learn about your husband’s hometown.</p><p>One of the principal spies was Caleb Brewster, an officer of the Continental army who grew up in Setauket, was an expert seaman and knew the Long Island Sound well. One of his acquaintances in town was Colonel Benjamin Tallmadge, who became Washington’s chief intelligence officer. Brewster was recruited by Tallmadge to spy on the British, who had occupied New York City as a base of operations.</p><p>Couriers traveled back and forth from New York, only 55 miles away, supplying Washington vital information about troop movements. They used coded messages in newspapers, an invisible ink called a “sympathetic strain,” to write between the lines of ordinary-looking letters, and a code book that assigned numbers to the principals. Washington was 711; Caleb Brewster was 725. A woman in town, Anna Strong, was said to have hung a black petticoat on a clothesline, alerting the network that Brewster was in town.</p><p>Caleb Brewster’s cousin, Joseph, ran the Brewster House, a tavern and general store which counted British soldiers as its customers. It still stands in town, right down the road from where Brown grew up.</p><p>“We live right near Brewster Road,’’ Brown said, another reason why he believes Washington may have stopped in what became the Brown homestead.</p><p>Does the name Benedict Arnold jar a memory from an American history class? The Culper Spy Ring is credited with helping to expose the conspiracy between a British major and the man who became synonymous with being a traitor, as Arnold schemed to deliver the fort at West Point to the Brits.</p><p>Brown, who is scheduled to start here Saturday night against the Cardinals, never daydreamed about being a spy.</p><p>“I was that crazy 10-year-old,’’ he said, “telling my entries.title: Is Sydney Taylor the answer to the Sky's struggling offense?
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" ><u>Sky</u></a> rookie Sydney Taylor has shown she can light it up off the bench. The question now is whether coach Tyler Marsh will grant her a bigger role.</p><p>The offense floundered in an 79-58 loss Friday against the Lynx at Wintrust Arena. The Sky have dropped four games in a row since losing leading scorer Rickea Jackson to a season-ending torn ACL.</p><p>So far, however, Marsh appears hesitant to fully embrace Taylor as the answer. After erupting for a team-high 27 points Wednesday against the Tempo, Taylor played only eight minutes in the first half against the Lynx.</p><p>Marsh said before the game that he thinks Taylor can be an answer ‘‘to some degree’’ for the loss of Jackson but that she’s still learning to play within his system and that there’s more to the equation than just scoring.</p><p>‘‘Rickea is tough shoes to fill for anyone,’’ he said. ‘‘We’ve got to make that up in all areas where we can, on both ends of the floor.’’</p><p>The Sky did tighten up their defense, holding the league-leading Lynx to fewer than 80 points. Defense has been the team’s calling card, so it makes sense that a microwave scorer isn’t necessarily Marsh’s first priority in the rotation.</p><p>Plus, Marsh is right that no one player will replace Jackson.</p><p>But the Sky do need to start getting creative offensively, at least until they’re fully healthy.</p><p>Against the Lynx, none of their key weapons — Kamilla Cardoso, Azura Stevens or Natasha Cloud — got going early. The passing was sloppy. They made only five of their 30 three-pointers.</p><p>Taylor can help give them a different look.</p><p>She has a filthy crossover and a jumper so serene you might get caught admiring it while it’s happening in your face. Most important, on a team Marsh says passes up too many shots, she’s always hunting for hers.</p><p>Her play made an impression on Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve. She read her players a stat — that Taylor had taken 22 shots in 23 minutes against the Tempo — to motivate them to defend her.</p><p>‘‘She has a real knack for putting the ball in the hole,’’ Reeve said. “She’s unafraid. She can change a game.</p><p>‘‘You talk about her, [but] it’s completely different when all of a sudden you get her on the court. You think you’re near her, and she’s shooting it.’’</p><p>Taylor played professionally in Poland before the Sky picked her up, and she has taken advantage of being relatively unknown in the WNBA.</p><p>‘‘That’s a perk of being a rookie: They’re not too familiar with my game,’’ she said at the shootaround Friday morning. ‘‘They were three, four or five feet off of me. I’m not used to that.’’</p><p>But the Lynx adjusted. Taylor took only two shots in the first half before sinking her first in the third quarter. She finished with seven points and four assists in 19 minutes.</p><p>Overall, she acknowledged she’s still figuring out how to fit her game to Marsh’s system and learn what he wants.</p><p>‘‘I’m used to being a heavy-scoring guard overseas, so [I’m] still trying to find that balance over here,’’ Taylor said. ‘‘I can score the ball at all levels, but [it’s] just knowing when to take shots in the offense, when my team needs me to score or when they need me to facilitate and find other people.’’</p><p>Taylor has plenty of room to grow, but she has the right attitude: a chip on her shoulder and hungry for more opportunities to prove herself.</p><p>‘‘I’m going out there like I’m still trying to make a roster spot every time I step on the floor,’’ she said. “Anytime I get in the game, it’s going to help me build my confidence. Just trying to get those minutes consistent.’’</p><p>Time will tell whether Marsh rewards it.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: A down-and-up night for Sox: Munetaka Murakami exits with injury before Miguel Vargas hits walk-off homer
entries.summary: <p>The swings of emotion for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> and their fans couldn’t have been more extreme on Friday night</p><p>Marquee slugger Munetaka Murakami left the game in the third inning with a right hamstring injury and likely is headed to the injured list. </p><p>But the Sox bounced back after being stymied at the plate most of the night and pulled off a thrilling 4-3 victory in 10 innings.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Munetaka Murakami left the game grabbing his hamstring <a href="https://t.co/29sWk7LV35">pic.twitter.com/29sWk7LV35</a></p>— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) <a href="https://x.com/TalkinBaseball_/status/2060520205550334007?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>They won it on Miguel Vargas 13<sup>th</sup> homer — a two-run, no-doubt line shot —  with two outs in the 10<sup>th </sup>after the Tigers had taked a 3-2 lead in the top of the frame on Zack Short’s deep sacrifice fly. Vargas launched his first career walk-off drive on a hanging changeup from Drew Anderson, setting off an on-field celebration and throaty roar from 30,019 fans.</p><p>The White Sox' third straight win moved them to 30-27 and three games over .500 for the first time since Sept. 21, 2022. At least for the moment, it assuaged the prospect of losing Murakami, tied for the American League lead in homers at 20, for an undetermined period.</p><p>“You know, since ‘Mune’ wasn’t in the game, I had to step up and take that, you know, power hit again. No just kidding,” Vargas quipped. “I just tried to drive the runner in (automatic runner Drew Romo) and put the team in a position where we can win the game.</p><p>“I got lucky. I got the right pitch. I put a good swing on it.”</p><p>Still, Murakami’s status loomed as a bigger concern.  The 26-year-old Japanese slugger, who signed a two-year, $34 million contract with the Sox in December, has been the No. 1 reason why the White Sox are both exciting and relevant again after three straight seasons of 101 or more losses. </p><p>Manager Will Venable didn’t have definite diagnosis, but he had an idea.</p><p>“Looks like a little hamstring strain on the initial evaluation,” Venable said. “He’ll get some imaging tomorrow, but probably a couple weeks.”</p><p>Murakami grabbed his the back of his right thigh, grimaced and walked slowly back to the dugout with Venable and training staff after running to first on a grounder that forced Sam Antonacci at second. The first-baseman was replaced by pinch-runner Luisangel Acuna, who scored the Sox first run on Vargas’ double. Vargas also took over for Murakami in the field, shifting from third.</p><p></p><p>Murakami didn’t leave the ballpark, however.</p><p>“We know the big piece that ‘Mune' is for the team and what he does for the team," Vargas said. “We all stay together and obviously he stayed there and was the first one in the clubhouse waiting for everyone. </p><p>“When you see that, it brings the group more together and closer. We all have to support him and hopefully it’s nothing bad.”</p><p>The South Siders' other Japanese player, Rikuu Nishida, played a role in sending the game to extra innings.</p><p>The Tigers led 2-1 entering the ninth. scoring both runs on catcher Dillon Dingler’s 11<sup>th</sup> homer in the third. He golfed Erick Fedde’s low changeup, not a mistake pitch, into the left field stands.</p><p>Detroit right-hander Troy Melton kept the Sox mostly off balance through the seventh, surrendering just one run on six hits in a second straight crisp start after coming off the 60-day IL with right forearm inflammation</p><p>Benintindi singled with one out in the ninth, then advanced to third on Tristan Peters' single. </p><p>Nishida bunted back to Tigers reliever Kyle Finnegan, who looked over his shoulder, then threw the speedy infielder/fielder out at first. But Finnegan never forced Benintendi back toward third, and he burst for home and slid in under a wide throw by Detroit first baseman Spencer Torkelson.</p><p>“Really heads-up play by Beni,” Venable said. “He’s been in those situations before, that’s what you get with a guy that has that kind of experience and that kind of baseball IQ.”</p><p>Injury depleted themselves, the Tigers dropped their 19<sup>th</sup> game in their of their last 23 in a dreadful May that has seen them plunge to 14 games below .500.</p><p> After just taking three of four games from Minnesota at on the South Side, the Sox improved to 9-3 against opponents from the American League Central.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><table class="cf wS" role="presentation" style="border-collapse: collapse;" entries.title: Calling foul on Pappas' Bears' megaproject bill analysis
entries.summary: <p>Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas released a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/26/bears-stadium-megaproject-bill-cook-county-treasurer-analysis" >“study” </a>last week about the state megaprojects proposal, including a new Bears stadium complex that was mostly uncritically received by local news media. But it’s not her best work, to say the least.</p><p>OK, before we go any further I should say I find corporate tax breaks distasteful and even sometimes counterproductive. I have no official or personal position on a deal to move the Chicago Bears to Arlington Heights (except for my personal hatred of Indiana). It’s just that “studies” like this make me cringe.</p><p>The report mainly focuses on the big bucks the Bears will save on their property tax bills if they move to the suburbs, which is pretty much the whole point of corporate subsidies.</p><p>Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, had the most obvious critique of the Pappas study.</p><p>“You can’t count full tax revenue from a project that doesn’t exist, may never get financed, may get tied up in court, or may go to another state,” the lead House megaprojects sponsor posted on social media. “The real choice is not ‘full taxes versus reduced taxes.’ The real choice is a negotiated payment on a real project, or full taxes on an empty lot.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4c0000" name="module-4c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>But that part of the Pappas report is just the usual critique of corporate subsidies, and while it’s not necessarily wrong, it simply refuses to accept the validity of corporate subsidies and goes for the “wow” factor to grab headlines, like this one from WTTW: “<a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/05/26/megaprojects-bill-would-mean-39m-annual-property-tax-break-bears-cook-county-treasurer-s" target="_blank" >‘Megaprojects’ Bill Would Mean a $39M Annual Property Tax Break for Bears.</a>”</p><p>Or, as Buckner said during a radio interview, “The report largely compares the bill against a fantasy baseline, where every project magically gets built and pays full taxes forever.”</p><p>To me, though, a big problem with Pappas’ report is it conveniently ignores or breezes past a few very important things:</p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-e9870461-5ba4-11f1-9e76-813a68cec346" start="1"><li><p> From the Pappas report about studies done on stadiums across the country: “Sports venues’ positive economic spillovers typically were confined to a relatively small area around the venue.”</p><p>But Pappas’ report fails to point out that the vast majority of the 326 acres of currently vacant Arlington Heights land will be developed into a year-round entertainment district, with hotels and other stuff. None of that land will be included in the megaproject district, so whatever is built will be assessed like any other property. And those additional property taxes could be a boon to the area.</p><p>As Pappas reports, Wrigley Field’s 2024 property tax bill was $3.9 million. But more than $10 million in property taxes were paid by “the team’s various other buildings around Wrigleyville.” I’m not saying the exact same thing will happen in Arlington Heights (the Pappas study estimates about $14 million a year in payments for the Bears stadium alone), I’m just saying it could be a lot of new money and that Pappas didn’t even bother to acknowledge it, even though the local governments are quite excited by this possible additional revenue stream.<br></p></li><li><p>The Pappas report asks: “Should the Illinois bill become law, one key question will remain: Would the amount of property taxes the team and any other megaproject developers end up paying be enough to cover the increased costs of education and other local services made necessary by their projects?”</p><p>But the report also very briefly mentions that all local governments including school districts would have weighted votes on approving the “payment in lieu of taxes” terms and amounts. Arlington Heights schools will have half the weighted vote based on taxes received. In most areas, school districts will have 60% of the weighted vote. More importantly, the legislation protects school district budgets from unforeseen expenses.</p><p>The state’s Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity is also involved in the approval process, and all the other legal hoops that companies must clear probably lessens the likelihood of a "monorail scam."<br></p></li><li><p>The report basically advocates for letting Indiana build the new stadium complex. Hammond is closer to Soldier Field than Arlington Heights, the study points out. That’s apples to oranges because one could argue that the team’s season-ticket holders live closer to Arlington Heights than Hammond.</p><p>The Indiana deal is obviously bad for their taxpayers, so Pappas suggests letting them pay for it if they’re gonna be so gullible.</p><p>But that seems more like advocacy than an actual study. And it ignores what a huge national spotlight on a very prominent Illinois entity moving across the border could trigger. If the Bears can do it, why not others?</p></li></ol><p>Again, I rarely go to Bears games so I really don’t care where they play. But I don’t claim my personal opinion is data.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-040000" name="module-040000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: South and West sides have highest rates of infant sleep deaths in Cook County
entries.summary: <p>Infants are dying about once a week on average in Cook County — most frequently on Chicago's South and West sides.</p><p>That's according to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.rush.edu/sites/default/files/media-documents/suid-report.pdf?utm_medium=email&utm_source=govdelivery" target="_blank" ><u>report</u></a> from Rush University Medical Center and the Cook County medical examiner's office, which identified 208 sudden and unexpected infant deaths between 2019 and 2023.</p><p>In October 2025, Rush University Medical in partnership with the Cook County medical examiner's office released the report using data from the Sudden Unexpected Infant Death-Case Registry.</p><p>U.S. Rep. Danny Davis joined medical professionals and community advocates Friday at the West Austin Child Development Center to raise awareness about Sudden Infant Death Syndrome and other sleep-related infant deaths.</p><p>For years, many of these deaths were categorized as SIDS because the exact cause was unclear, said Dr. Gina Lowell, the study's principal investigator. But a closer examination of the cases revealed a common pattern.</p><p>“When we looked at our babies, our 208 babies who died here in Cook County from 2019 to 2023, we found that the majority of them were in adult beds or on couches,” Lowell said.</p><p>Lowell warned during the news conference that those numbers are rising — projecting that there were 52 sleep-related deaths in 2025.</p><p>The report found sleep-related infant deaths happened most frequently in South and West side communities facing higher levels of poverty, crowded housing, unemployment and educational disparities.</p><p>“You may not have the bandwidth to remember how to place your baby asleep to save their life when you're already thinking about saving your family's life in so many other ways,” Lowell said.</p><p>Tamera Fair, CEO of Premier Child Care facilities in the Chicago area, said sometimes “bonding can turn into a crisis in a nanosecond.”</p><p>"We had a family who was breastfeeding," Fair said. "The mother rolled over on the baby, and that baby died. That was a tragedy for every family here at West Austin Child Development."</p><p>Felicia Clark, prevention coordinator for CPASS Chicago and a former child death investigator with the Cook County medical examiner's office, said oftentimes parents mimic the habits of their matriarchs.</p><p>"Families will always say, 'I didn't think it could happen to me. I slept with my baby, my mom slept with me,'" Clark said. "Behind every statistic is a baby who was loved and a family whose life has been forever changed."</p><p>The report also found Black infants died due to a sleep-related deaths at a rate 14 times higher than white infants, and the rate was 2.3 times higher among Hispanic infants than white infants.</p><p>Clark said the good news is that most sleep-related infant deaths are preventable.</p><p>Health experts recommend that babies sleep alone, on their backs and in a crib, bassinet or play yard with a firm mattress and fitted sheet. Parents should avoid couches, adult beds, blankets, pillows, stuffed animals and other loose items in a baby's sleep space.</p><p>“If we can ensure babies can breathe easy, we will prevent these deaths,” Lowell said. “If we can guard their breathing, make it easy for our babies to breathe, we'll save their lives.”<br></p>

entries.title: Cubs done with 10-game skid, but can they learn from losing streak in season of extremes?
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — What sort of mindset do the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> have in the wake of a 10-game losing streak?</p><p>“The rest of the story is yet to be written, and it can be written in any sort of way. None of us know how it’s going to go,” lefty starter Matthew Boyd told the Sun-Times on Friday. “But I tell you what, we all do believe we are, if not the best team, one of the best teams in baseball.”</p><p>Well, it didn’t ding their confidence.</p><p>The extended losing stretch <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/27/timely-home-runs-help-cubs-end-10-game-losing-streak" >came to a merciful end Wednesday night in Pittsburgh</a>, but the shock of a 10-game skid that followed a pair of 10-game winning streaks has fans feeling whiplash.</p><p>This season has been less a roller-coaster ride and more a Tower of Terror. Roller coasters have inclines and declines. The Cubs have gone straight up and, more recently, straight down.</p><p>“This has been a more extreme baseball team,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said before Friday’s loss to the rival Cardinals. “If you do this long enough, you think it’s going to be very even, and sometimes it’s not. We’ve got to live with that.”</p><p>The Cubs would prefer things to be slightly less jarring from here on out. They have championship-level expectations and will need to build some consistency over a lengthy summer of baseball if they’re going to meet them.</p><p>They are no longer, according to the standings, what Boyd says they are, one of the best teams in the sport. They left that distinction behind with the slide.</p><p>They are playing a rival Redbird group — supposedly rebuilding but doing enough winning that they’re jockeying with the Cubs in the all-teams-above-.500 NL Central — with work to do to get back to the top of the heap.</p><p>If the Cubs are going to do what they were projected to — not only dispatching of these upstart Cardinals but also somehow finding a way to topple the first-place Brewers — they’ll need to take a lesson or two from the 10-game nightmare.</p><p>“You never want to go through them, but it’s those valleys that do make you better,” Boyd said. “It’s times like that 10-game losing streak that you can look back on and use it to make yourself better and move forward and say, ‘Let’s make adjustments and grow from these things and, hopefully, not let them happen again.’ ”</p><p>“These kinds of things, they almost bring you a little bit closer,” designated hitter <b>Michael Conforto</b> told the Sun-Times. “Everybody had a rough patch in there, and when those things happen, you’ve got guys picking each other up and meeting up to talk about the game, talk about what’s not going right. It’s an opportunity for the guys to get even closer than they were before, going through something like that.”</p><p><b>Can’t keep ’em in the yard</b></p><p>The Cubs have a problem on their hands as May nears its conclusion: baseball’s most homer-prone pitching staff, which came into Friday having allowed a league-worst 79 home runs. Then lefty starter <b>Shota Imanaga</b> grew that number, surrendering a trio of round trippers in his team’s 6-5 defeat.</p><p>That’s eight homers allowed in the last three starts for Imanaga — during which he owns an enormous 11.49 ERA — bringing to mind his late-season struggles last year, when he allowed 15 homers over his last nine regular-season starts and three more in a pair of playoff appearances.</p><p><b>Itching to pitch</b></p><p>Sidelined for weeks while recovering from knee surgery, Boyd, the Cubs’ Opening Day starter, will make a rehab start with Triple-A Iowa on Sunday. Suffice to say, he’s ready to get back on the mound.</p><p>“I’m super excited to just go compete,” he said. “You try to compete in everything you do, whether it’s rehab or in a game. It’s a lot more fun to do it between the white lines.”<br>id. “You try to compete in everything you do, whether it’s rehab or in a game.
